quote: Wenn zwei Massenpunkte nach dem Newtonschen Gesetze auf ein- ander wirken und [-...-] in derselben Geraden aufeinander zu sich be- wegen, wie laufen sie dann durch einander durch?
english: If two mass points act on each other according to Newton's law and move toward each other along the same straight line, how do they then pass through each other?
topic: The page notes Nernst's diffusion problem with a closed-form solution, a question about two Newtonian mass points colliding along a line, questions about minimum principles in optics and Maxwell's electrodynamics, and the start of a remark on Poincaré's idea of periodic cycles on Riemann surfaces.

triage.modern_statement: Two point masses attract each other by Newton's inverse-square law and move head-on along one line (the rectilinear, or 1-dimensional, Kepler problem: for the relative distance x, x'' = -k/x^2). The solution reaches x = 0 in finite time, and at that moment the speed becomes infinite. The question is how the motion should be continued through this binary collision, and whether there is a natural way to do it. In modern terms this is the problem of regularizing binary collisions in the two-body and N-body problems. A key sub-question is whether the natural continuation is an elastic bounce (x stays positive) or the bodies passing through each other (x changes sign).
triage.answered_by: This is the classical topic of collision regularization in celestial mechanics. Levi-Civita (1903; and his 1920 regularization of the perturbed planar two-body problem), Bisconcini (1906) and Sundman (1907, 1909, 1912) worked on it, and it was later extended by others such as Kustaanheimo and Stiefel. The standard answer is that near collision the distance behaves like r(t) ~ |t|^(2/3), and that the solution has a natural continuation through the singularity: analytic continuation onto another sheet of the Riemann surface of r(t). In the regularized flow (Levi-Civita substitution x = u^2) the bodies bounce back elastically. In relative coordinates that differs from passing through only in which body is which. None of the sources I found refers to Hilbert's note. The bounce-versus-pass-through point is the standard textbook view of Levi-Civita regularization and is not spelled out in the snippets I retrieved.

evidence.claim: Levi-Civita (1903), Bisconcini (1906) and Sundman (1907, 1909, 1912) were the main early researchers on regularizing collisions between two bodies; Sundman used his binary-collision results in his complete series solution of the three-body problem (1912).

Painlevé (1895) showed that binary and triple collisions are the only possible singularities in the three-body problem. Levi-Civita then tried to regularize collisions by a change of variables, and the 1D Kepler ODE x'' = -k/x^2, which is singular at x = 0, is the model example.

Waldvogel's survey treats rectilinear parabolic Kepler motion explicitly: the collision solution has a natural continuation from its past through the singularity, and this continuation corresponds to analytic continuation onto a different sheet of the Riemann surface. The survey also covers Levi-Civita's 1920 regularization.
Levi-Civita regularization removes binary-collision singularities in perturbed planar Kepler problems, and Heggie extended it to all three binary collisions of the three-body problem at once.

Related collinear collision questions are still being researched, for example how smooth the regularized flow is near simultaneous binary collisions in the collinear 4-body problem (the conjectured C^(8/3) bound).

triage.why: Hilbert's question about how two Newtonian point masses on a line 'pass through each other' at collision matches the binary-collision regularization problem. Levi-Civita, Sundman and others addressed it in roughly 1903–1920, and it is now standard in celestial mechanics. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The basic two-body case is settled: the continuation is unique and natural (analytic continuation / regularization, giving an elastic bounce). Regularization of more complicated collisions (simultaneous binary collisions, triple collisions, collinear N-body problems) is still an active research area. Confidence is medium for three reasons: the note itself is short and its date is not given, no source links Hilbert's note to this literature, and the identification rests on matching the content.
